item.title: How to Build Skull Archfiend of Chaos in Yu-Gi-Oh's Genesys Format
item.description:
Yu-Gi-Oh!|Genesys|competitive

How to Build Skull Archfiend of Chaos in Yu-Gi-Oh's Genesys Format

Try some crazy lines and bridge the gap between Fiends and Sacred Beasts with Hanko's Genesys latest brew.

By Hanko Chow

|

Published Sep 30, 2026

|

11 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Recently, I was fortunate enough to participate in the Latin American Remote YCS. While I do usually tend to avoid this kind of event since I believe it was meant to be for Latin American participants, I just wanted to find the most competitive and accessible event to try my new deck at. I would like to thank the tournament organizers and judges for their patience with me and allowing me to play even though I don't speak their native language. Even though I won all three of the last rounds of Swiss in day two, I unfortunately only finished ninth due to tiebreakers. Nonetheless, I'm still pretty happy with my performance with this deck and I'm excited to showcase it!

How to Build Skull Archfiend of Chaos in Genesys

The idea of the deck started out with the realization of how broken Skull Archfiend of Chaos really is as a package. This monster, when it goes to the graveyard, activates to send the Ritual Spell for cost to add another Ritual Monster. Sending Light and Darkness Ritual allows you to add Magician of Dark Chaos - Black Chaos, which can later help you reuse a Spell, or Black Luster Soldier - Soldier of Light and Darkness, which can be a hassle for some decks to deal with. Somehow, Skull Archfiend of Chaos is unpointed in Genesys while there's only five points on Light and Darkness Ritual. Getting Skull Archfiend of Chaos into the graveyard is easy depending on the deck. If it's in your hand or you have a copy of Fiendish Rhino Warrior, any way to discard them to the graveyard will trigger it. This is doable with Fusion Summoning or the next most popular engine right now in Genesys, the Sacred Beast retrains from Chaos Origins.

Calamity of the Sacred Beasts - Hamon, Lord of Striking Thunder, Infinity of the Sacred Beasts - Raviel, Lord of Phantasms and especially Sacred Beasts Released are all very low pointed cards, with only two each on the Hamon and Raviel retrains and surprisingly no points on the Spell that searches for three cards! By using these cards alongside Summoner of the Sacred Beasts (five points), you can easily summon two Sacred Beasts and sometimes draw two cards off Fallen Paradise of the Sacred Beasts before Xyz Summoning Varudras, the Final Bringer of the End Times (20 points) for the destructive omni-negate. This concept of combining Sacred Beasts and Skull Archfiend of Chaos is slowly trending to top tables since it gives you an immense amount of card advantage in your hand while also summoning huge threats! For only five points, any deck can summon these Ritual Monsters that are unaffected by card effects unless they target them.

Unfortunately, you won't always have access to Skull Archfiend of Chaos in the Sacred Beast build unless you also commit points to playing Mercurium the Living Quicksilver (10 points). This also means you'll want to play the other Sacred Beast support cards like Martyr of the Sacred Beasts and Sacred Beasts Thunderclap, which both cost three points per card. By attaching the Skull Archfiend of Chaos to Mercruium, and then sending it for the Field Spell effect, you almost get the same value as when you start with both. I wasn't a big fan of this version since it seems too costly to play. I wanted a deck that can afford to play all the best and affordable hand traps in the Genesys metagame. Mulcharmy Fuwalos (eight points each) is a must-have even though it's not good against Blitzclique, while Skull Meister, D.D. Crow (two points each) and Ghost Ogre & Snow Rabbit (four points each) are all great in most matchups.

With that in mind, I still wanted to focus on taking advantage of Skull Archfiend of Chaos and the Light and Darkness Ritual package. This led me to the next best synergy in the format - Chimera Fusion. This concept has already been showing success since YCS Montreal with the likes of Kyle Waterman and Ram Sighn's builds. Mirror Swordknight is one of the strongest Normal Summons in the game, so I built my own version of it to try it out.

After building these decks separately, I came to the realization that I could just put these two concepts together. By taking out the costly Martyr of the Sacred Beasts Normal Summon and the bricky Sacred Beasts Thunderclap, I built a pile which I personally believe to feature the lowest amount of point costs for the highest reward value. After testing the 60-card build for a while, I found a way to bridge Chimera Fusion cards into Sacred Beasts so long as I open up the Skull Archfiend of Chaos or Fiendish Rhino Warrior with my Mirror Swordknight or Gazelle the King of Mythical Claws. Unfortunately there isn't a real bridge from Sacred Beasts into Chimera Fusion, but you'll often just draw into the Chimera cards from Fallen Paradise of the Sacred Beasts or win without them. Here's the list I brought to the Latin American Remote YCS!

Skull Archfiend of Chaos Decklist

Here's a brief summary of the game plan: the Normal Summon is Mirror Swordknight or Gazelle the King of Mythical Claws, which are very powerful when you combine them with Skull Archfiend of Chaos or any Fiend since you can eventually use Berfomet the Mythical King of Phantom Beasts to send the Skull Archfiend of Chaos or any other valuable piece to connect the engines. If you open with Sacred Beast cards, you can make Varudras, the Final Bringer of the End Times without your Normal Summon while also drawing two cards off Fallen Paradise of the Sacred Beasts.

Both engines are high value and if you open both engines, you can make an incredibly near-invincible end board that can potentially even out play popular board breakers like The Winged Dragon of Ra - Sphere Mode or Lava Golem since there are a lot of layered interactions.

I say it's nearly invincible because the end board also features the Diabell duo package since Gazelle can search for Diabellze the White Witch, which is very easy to summon and filters you through Curse of Diabell and Filia Diabell to get the necessary banishes for Diabellstar Vengeance. Having both Vengeance and White Witch on field will grant your monsters protection from destruction effects while Magician of Dark Chaos - Black Chaos protects your Spell and Traps, making your end board indestructible so that Blitzclique can't touch you.

Not only that, but we're backing it up with Varudras, the Final Bringer of the End Times for the omni-negate and even D/D/D Wave High King Caesar (20 points) to negate two Special Summon activations since it's the best value for two Level 6 Fiends. The backrow will usually have Chimera Fusion and maybe even Sacred Beasts Combined Assault in case you need Inferno of the Sacred Beasts - Uria, Lord of Searing Flames's Spell Trap removal or Hamon to protect your life points.

Starting the game off with Chimera the King of Phantom Beasts not only takes away a random card from your opponent's hand but having that reborn effect during your opponent's turn will either cost them a Skull Meister or can reborn something useful. Usually they'll want to break the destruction protection from the Diabell duo so reborning one of them with the Chimera can be useful. Alternatively, if there's a scenario where multiple monsters get cleared, you can technically summon Infinity of the Sacred Beasts - Raviel, Lord of Phantasms with the Chimera so that Sacred Beasts Combined Assault can also be an omni-negate.

Chimera Fusion is also very useful as another method of disruption depending on the scenario. The most common Fusion I summon has to be the new Nightmare-Eyes Restrict as it takes any combination between Spellcaster, Fiend or Illusion to summon and will equip a monster without targeting. Since Magician of Dark Chaos - Black Chaos is a Spellcaster, this Fusion is easy to make, especially if the opponent is throwing a Lava Golem, Santa Claws or their own Radian, the Multidimensional Kaiju onto my field, all of which are Fiends. Predaplant Dragostapelia or even Azamina Sol Erysichthon may also be necessary depending on the situation.

After I make this end board and rip a random card out of my opponent's hand, I usually win the game since there's almost no card combination that can beat all of my unique interactions. I have nearly a 100 percent win rate whenever I draw a combination of Chimera cards and Sacred Beasts. It's possible to draw less optimally at times which luckily only happened a few times throughout this event for me, but even the half boards you make can surprisingly win.

Another reason why I wanted to play this combination of engines is because of how the metagame of Genesys was in the Side Deck. Many players will have targeted hate towards the Sacred Beast cards like The Eye of Truth or Mutually Affured Destruction, so having the Chimera and Ritual of Light and Darkness cards as a secondary method to play helps compliment the deck. It worked out in my favor at times since it also messed up the opponent's Side Deck plan. Now they either side in more cards than they wanted to or draw the wrong ones depending on which part of my deck I open up to play with.

The Bridge Between Chimera and Sacred Beasts

As previously mentioned, there's a way to bridge or search yourself a Sacred Beast card from only having Chimera Fusion cards and the resources from Skull Archfiend of Chaos. Ideally you'll open a combination of either Mirror Swordknight or Gazelle the King of Mythical Claws with either Skull Archfiend of Chaos or Fiendish Rhino Warrior.

In a slightly convoluted method, you'll aim to send a copy of Infinity of the Sacred Beasts - Raviel, Lord of Phantasms alongside Buio the Dawn's Light, which searches for Mutiny in the Sky. You'll gain access to this double send by using Gazelle the King of Mythical Claws's effect to search for any Illusion monster to search for Fleeting Phantom Mask Master instead of the Diabellze. This makes your end board less powerful than if you already had access to the Sacred Beast cards to begin with, but I would feel that a potential omni-negate or two is more valuable than the Diabell duo at times.

By having both Mutiny in the Sky in our hands and the copy of Raviel in the graveyard, you simply need to use Mutiny in the Sky to Fusion summon for The Duke of Demise, then use the Mutiny in the Sky's graveyard effect to send the Duke of Demise to add it back. Now you can use the Duke's graveyard effect to banish itself to recover Raviel! Raviel will search for Hamon, which gets you to Sacred Beasts Released, and you'll be able to access Summoner of the Sacred Beasts and Inferno of the Sacred Beasts - Uria, Lord of Searing Flames to eventually Xyz Summon a Varudras, the Final Bringer of the End Times.

As an aside, while I was studying these possible lines and seeing what I can do with the power of sending any Fiend to the graveyard, I rediscovered the Sky Scourge Norleras and Phantom of Chaos combo, but since we can't just use any two monsters to make Muckraker From the Underworld in Genesys, I had to find another way to get the Phantom of Chaos onto the field. This required the use of Constellar Ptolemy M7 and the extra Normal Summon you get from The Duke of Demise! Maybe someday I could use this combo in Genesys if they don't increase the points on the Chimera Fusion cards.

Deck Building Should Be Fun in Genesys!

I honestly can't wait for the next points update for Genesys. I really hope they increase the frequency of these points update after every YCS since I find the format being solved less appealing to me than when it's unsolved. I did notice their latest blog post addressed how they're going to reevaluate the initial points list from last year, which I'm excited for! Hopefully they reduce the points enough and let me play Floowandereeze as another deck that represents the Tribute Summon mechanic. Having only Monarchs and Clown Crew represent it feels a bit too restricted, especially since Monarchs have received a ton of nerfs over this year.

I also think that Ghost Mourner & Moonlit Chill can go down to four points since I do think it has potential in the format if it was just one point cheaper. Making it cost the same as Ghost Ogre & Snow Rabbit could be interesting. Another random wish I have is if they can find a way to reduce the points on several other banned cards, like Soul Charge being at 50 is just a bit too much. Maybe it can be 35 to 40 points to make it more viable. Even Pot of Greed isn't seeing too much play anymore at 30 points, but I don't know if that's a good comparison.

Those are my thoughts before the new banlist drops. Hopefully you enjoyed this Fiend pile! I did manage to record a deck profile of it so be sure to check that out if you want a bit more insight on what I played. For now, I'll be looking into what Beyond the Brave gives us to make Genesys more interesting!

Written By

item.title: How to Play Levia in Silver Age
item.description:
Flesh and Blood|competitive

How to Play Levia in Silver Age

Satiate your hunger with Karol's guide to the returning Shadow Brute!

By Karol Ruszkiewicz

|

Published Oct 2, 2026

|

6 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Levia has shown up as a huge contender this Silver Age season, securing three placements in the Top 8 thanks to the efforts of Jacob Clements, Francesco Giorgio, and Kilian Schellekens. I've scoured through these decklists to find which cards are must-includes and what tech the different players have sprinkled in.

Levia already had some great common and rare cards in the past. Dread Screamer, Boneyard Marauder, Endless Maw, and Graveling Growl have all been incredible at punching through raw damage. However, the way these work, it takes some time to get enough cards into the graveyard, let alone enough 6-power attack action cards to consistently play these out while satisfying Levia's blood debt.

In terms of previous equipment, Hooves of the Shadowbeast has been a monster of a leg piece, being extremely flexible in granting not only an attack go again, but also an action point as long as you have a card to banish. That's it. Banish a 6-power card and you can convert your boots into a clean action point. Beaten Trackers...but better?

More recently, Compendium of Rathe introduced further power cards in the form of Embraforged Gauntlet, Engulfing Shadows, and Pound of Flesh.

On the Brute side, we also received some top-tier pieces of equipment that play really well into Levia's game plan. Buzzard Helm helps fix awkward hands, such as drawing four reds, while also filling up the graveyard to enable the old-school Shadow Brute attacks.

Predatory Plating also offers great defensive value and a precious resource when it matters. And it can matter a lot.

Levia's curve often uses 2-cost cards with go again, meaning two blues are perfect for playing out three of these in a row, often performing her iconic attack for 6, then 6, then 6. However, sometimes you're only able to attack twice, and 4 can be an awkward amount of pitch. This is why we see these lists include Vigorous Smashup in yellow and blue, with some running all six available copies. Vigor and top-deck manipulation are crucial for smoothing out certain turns, especially when combined with the toys Levia just received in Usurp the Shadow Throne...

So what makes Levia so good all of a sudden?

Firstly, it's the new attacks.

Big Bonkers

What's better than some over-rate attacks? A whole lot more over-rate attacks! Not only that, but ones that don't require a busy graveyard to get going.

Feeding Frenzy and Feasting Shadowbeast are all-star attacks that not only match the efficiency of the Monarch attacks, but are also much easier to enable. Their effects are satisfied by any banish, not just their own. This means they make great follow-up cards and can also be enabled by cards like Hex Gauntlet and Cleave the Heavens.

Gates to i'Arathael

Cleave the Heavens isn't just a pretty face. It creates one of the most important components of Levia's toolkit: Gates to i'Arathael, a token that unlocks "free" cards from banish. As the game goes on, you'll have more and more juicy targets for these Gates, allowing you to throw out attacks with unparalleled efficiency.

Being able to convert a single blue into a Feasting Shadowbeast for 8 while satisfying blood debt is incredible, especially in Silver Age. Gates are particularly effective against slower decks that give you time to set up big turns and the space to build a hefty banish zone. I recommend leaning further into setting up Gates with cards like Rites of Nightfall, Countdown to Extinction, and more copies of Cleave the Heavens if your local metagame likes to take it slow.

Blasmophet, the Insatiable Hunger

The big demon makes his way into Silver Age! Blasmophet, the Insatiable Hunger offers an amazing package against a wide range of decks. Cards like Goremass Summoning, Beckoning Hunger, and Rumbling Hunger are the main ways to get the demon into the arena, and that is one scary on-hit. If your opponent lets this one through, it can take over the game.

While Gates offer a similar effect, not having to pitch that extra resource and having the effect on tap means you can continue playing free cards from banish, as long as you feed the beast, that is.

Blasmophet's upkeep requires you to continue banishing Shadow cards. Luckily, on your turn you're most likely doing that anyway to satisfy your hero ability. However, it's a bit trickier to do so on your opponent's turn. Some cards fulfill this condition themselves. Cleave the Heavens, Embraforged Gauntlet, and Engulfing Shadows all banish Shadow cards in one form or another.

Some cards also benefit from having a Blasmophet in play. The most played one is Consuming Command, a power play if you have it in your banish zone while controlling a Blasmophet. For 1 resource, you get to attack for 6 with go again, and the best thing is that if you continue to load it with graveyard-banishing effects, you can continue to attack with it. Most lists run only one copy, as that seems to be all you need to get the loop going.

Metagaming

There are a few cards that stood out to me, as they made some lists but not others.

Kilian's build seems the most resilient to fatigue strategies. Including two copies of Howl from Beyond opens up a constant loop of power. You play out the Howl, buff up your attack, then banish it from the graveyard with a Dread Screamer or Boneyard Marauder.

Jacob Clements is a big fan of Agility. Including a Test of Agility and Clash of Agility means that, as long as he can win those clashes, he can make these already incredibly efficient attacks even better by giving them go again. Smashback Alehorn offers even more go again and extra power, making it a great setup card for creating explosive turns.

Another point of contention is whether the lists should run Consuming Lash or Consuming Strength. As a general rule of thumb, I'd say go again is more likely to be useful against slower decks, while the extra +2 power pairs nicely with on-hit attacks like Rumbling Hunger and Beckoning Hunger, especially against aggressive decks that don't want to be defending.

Closing Thoughts

Despite just entering this new metagame, these players have turned up with incredibly tuned decks and a strategy for anything their opponents might throw at them.

I hope you got plenty of useful information on how to pilot Levia, because she is not only a highly competitive deck, but also a delightful puzzle to solve each and every game.

item.title: The Best-Selling Cards in Disney Lorcana Right Now - September 2026
item.description:
Disney Lorcana|finance

The Best-Selling Cards in Disney Lorcana Right Now - September 2026

Rapunzel? What is this, 2025?!

By Scott Mines

|@HowlingMines
|

Published Oct 2, 2026

|

7 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

It's been a hectic month for Disney Lorcana as the road to Hyperia City marches forward.We're about to enter a wondrous world blending music and art with the fantastical whimsy of heroes and princesses, introducing the much-beloved Coco to the game for the very first time. The setis also stuffed with fan-favourite franchises like Zootopia, Gargoyles and A Goofy Movie, and sounsurprisingly has been stealing most of the spotlight as we get closer to release. 

But we've also had a ton of play to follow at both the local level and tournament tables. Between the North American Championship, European Championship and Brazilian Championship, the metagame has been shifting almost every week. In fact, I still can't confidently tell you what the best deck in the format is! 

Well, you know what they say: When in doubt, trust Frank Karsten. 

But clearly the community has its own plans! Between speculatory purchases that are synergistic with new reveals from Hyperia City, a continued reinvigoration of the collecting aspect of the game and a variety of viable decks at the top of the metagame, it's been incredibly fun to chunk though the bestsellers data this month. 

You wanna see what everybody has been buying? I thought you might. Let's chat about the best-selling cards in Disney Lorcana throughout September 2026. 

#10 Lilo & Stitch - Fun-Loving Friends

The dynamic duo may have been crashing in price, but that hasn't slowed interest in the Amber Steel lynchpin. Lilo & Stitch - Fun-Loving Friends provides an absurd rate on an early character that's more than happy to shift in and sing He Hurled His Thunderbolt. 

The card isn't flashy, but it doesn't need to be. All the numbers here are great, and the only reason it isn't seeing more play is because it's ink-locked to Amber Steel. As the format adjusts to allow one of the better OG combinations to flourish, we'll see plenty of Lilo & Stitch. It makes sense that players are grabbing them while they're cheap! 

#9 Milo Thatch - Getting His Hands Dirty

On the other end of the spectrum, Milo Thatch has been getting his hands dirty. The card continues to be on the up-and-up as Amber Emerald Songs/Circle of Life and the infamous Emerald Sapphire Mouse House continue to find their footing at the tournament tables. 

Ward is such a big draw in an interactive format, but a three-pip threat that's also forcing discards and generating cards is a whole different beast. I'm glad to see Milo Thatch - Getting His Hands Dirty finally having his moment in the sun and I'm not expecting it to end post-Hyperia City. In fact, ink drops probably just elevate what Milo is capable of. 

#8 Gaston - Superior Archer

It's a continued fall from grace for Gaston - Superior Archer, who already stumbled from the best-selling card in Attack of the Vine! to a second-place finish last month. However, this isn't because the card became bad overnight — quite the opposite. I just think that most players have secured their copies of Gaston at this point. 

We're still shooting down many of the biggest threats in Core Constructed with a well-stated, inkable bow. Much like Lilo & Stitch (who conveniently support Gaston), I expect the play rate for this card to only increase as we enter metagames where it truly shines. 

If anything, you should see this as a sign that you're lacking behind if you haven't spent your three bucks to pick these up yet. 

#7 Winnie the Pooh & Piglet - Hunny Mages

This is adorable to see and brings me joy. I'm curious how much of this acceleration of sales for Winnie the Pooh & Piglet - Hunny Mages comes from [Format Coconut], where it's even easier to find yourself with multiple ink colors in play.

There's also a chance that cards from the Hundred-Acre Wood are seeing an uptick of sales to align with their hundred-year anniversary, which sees several news books releasing about our honey-loving friend. Otherwise, I can only see this as another signpost of the popularity of duo cards, which have consistently appeared on our bestseller lists since they were released in Attack of the Vine!. 

I'll be curious to see if this one can hold the momentum going forward. 

#6 Woody & Buzz Lightyear - Best Buddies

Another duo rocking the list, Woody & Buzz Lightyear - Best Buddies feels like its waiting for the right moment to strike at the tournament tables. Amber Emerald Toys doesn't quite have the oomph to hold its own with other archetypes in those inks right now, but it feels like it's only a matter of time. After all, toys are still a relatively new thing. 

That said, this is yet another endorsement of the increasing casual side of the collector's market in Disney Lorcana. Woody and Buzz aren't worth a fortune in their base rarity, but Disney fans simply want to own cards that feature their favorite characters and that's a lovely thing. 

#5 Mushu - Stealthy Dragon

Attack of the Vine's most expensive legendary continues to move units month-on-month, but it's a significant fall from first to fifth. I'm sure the previous sales numbers play a part in this slow decline, but the card has also fallen out of favor from some Emerald Steel and Emerald Amethyst pilots. 

That said, it's still a powerhouse. Mushu - Stealthy Dragon is a must-answer threat that has warped the format around the format, and it'll likely continue to create those metagame vortexes at several points until it rotates. 

You're just going to want to own copies of Mushu at some point in the next twelve months, and under ten bucks seems a good time to make sure that happens. 

#4 Mickey Mouse - Bob Cratchit

Okay, I'm gonna try to keep my personal biases in check on this one. There's definitelyno need to call anyone a "monster" or some other name... and it definitely doesn't get worse further up this list. 

If you couldn't tell, I'm not the biggest fan of Emerald Sapphire Mouse House. I can't deny that the deck is exactly that — a house. Quick lore and Ward characters are a surefire recipe for game wins, and we're seeing more players than ever lean on Mickey Mouse - Bob Cratchit as the best rodent to enable the namesake threat: Mickey Mouse & Minnie Mouse - Adventuring Duo.

The base rarity is up an eyewatering 756% in the last thirty days as copies on the market start to thin. If you want the epic variant, you're looking at $33 a copy at this point. Bruh.

#3 Dr. Bushroot - Evil Botanist

Disney Lorcana players out here showing their true colors in September... and they're green and blue. 

Dr. Bushroot - Evil Botanist is one of the standard Ward options available to Emerald Sapphire Mouse House, ripping away the limited tools the opponent has to challenge you as they desperately try to shut down your removal-proof-huge-pip board of characters. It's not flashy, but it achieves that role incredibly well. 

At seventy cents, it's hard to complain really. Dr. Bushroot will continue to sell en-masse for as long as more players gravitate towards Emerald Sapphire for their events. Will Hyperia City add more tools for the archetype? We'll have to wait and see. 

#2 Mickey Mouse & Minnie Mouse - Adventuring Duo

Of course. Who else could it be? 

You don't become the namesake of a deck without making some cheddar. Mickey Mouse & Minnie Mouse - Adventuring Duo continue to climb month-on-month as their budget-friendly deck flourishes in popularity. 

We previously saw the price of the card cascading towards $10 each as word got around, but it's currently at a much more affordable $4 despite the surge in popularity. I can't shake the feeling that this price chart is going to look like a rollercoaster by the end of the year. 

But who kept the lovable duo off the throne? Well. 

#1 Rapunzel - Escaping the Tower (Store Championship Promo)

That's right, specifically the Store Championship participant version of Rapunzel - Escaping the Tower. Strange, huh? 

This card has clearly become a target for speculation for a portion of the market that feel it is massively undervalued at just $2. It has sold almost double the amount of any other Disney Lorcana card on the TCGplayer marketplace this month, which is frankly an astounding stat. 

I can see the vision. The card has already seen a smattering of play in various Elinor - Renowned Diplomat decks and carries a stat line and type line that will continue to overperform. If you don't want to shell out thirty bucks for the shiny copies (or simply didn't win them) then there's no better version of the card to own. 

Heaven forbid we see a Shift Rapunzel in Hyperia City. That'd make this card go nuclear.

Disney Lorcana's [Format Coconut] Could Rival Commander

By Peter Day

item.title: Top 10 Best-Selling Presales From Magic: The Gathering Reality Fracture
item.description:
Magic: The Gathering|collecting|finance

Top 10 Best-Selling Presales From Magic: The Gathering Reality Fracture

The votes are in, and the Pyromancer is on fire.

By Emma Partlow

|

Published Oct 2, 2026

|

8 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Bestselling Cards of the Week

It's been almost six months since we've had an in-universe Magic: The Gathering release, but Reality Fracture has everything to become one of the most memorable yet. There's colorful twists and turns on popular characters, such as Fblthp who finally found the way out of Ravnica to Karn nurturing a Mirrodin without the Phyrexians ever existing. Reality Fracture really does ask the question "What If?", bringing with it a plethora of exciting cards geared towards competitive and casual play. 

Top 10 Best-Selling Presales From Magic: The Gathering Reality Fracture

There's been a bunch of sales activity leading up to Reality Fracture's release, but there's always a few cards on the bubble that are worth keeping in mind when making those orders. Samut, Hazoret's Champion is one such card, and comes with an elegant bit of text to grant all creatures you control haste. This isn't anything fancy for sure, but it will be a popular addition in Commander as this is the best on-rate haste enabler printed thus far. 

A similar sentiment applies to Avacyn, Angel of Horror, which happens to be the best-selling card from the Commander: Reality Fracture subset. Avacyn is a much-loved character from Magic's deep history, with her Echoverse version introducing a potent way to recur nontoken creatures you control back to the battlefield upon dying. It's rather on-theme, and will serve well in any black-based Commander decks moving forward. Cruel Calculations may be close to bulk pricing already, but it's another card seeing interest as it has a high ceiling in Mill-based Commander strategies. Apparently rewarding yourself with card draw when you're milling three players seems to be a good rate. With the trends out of the way, let's look at the best-selling cards from Reality Fracture leading up to today's highly-anticipated release. 

#10 Samut, Tyrant of Naktamun

If there's one card that has seen widespread discussion and discourse leading up to Reality Fracture's release, it's Samut, Tyrant of Naktamun. 

Split second is a keyword ability we don't see often and for a very good reason: it means players can't cast spells or activate abilities once a spell with split second hits the stack. This has potential implications for competitive Commander (cEDH), as the format is highly interactive and the utilizing the stack is foundational for gameplay reasons. That said, Samut is extremely soft to an Orcish Bowmasters trigger or two.

It's unclear whether this version of Samut will have the negative impact on Commander as discussed extensively online, but presales dictate that players are keen to find out for themselves. Giving instants and sorceries split second reads inherently powerful, but time will tell if the card lives up to the discussion.

#9 Draconic Visitor

Draconic Visitor is a color bend on Divine Visitation, a popular Commander card that turns any token you create into an evasive threat. As the name suggests, Draconic Visitor converts any artifact token you create into a 5/5 Dragon instead, which has exciting applications alongside Smaug the Magnificent and Smaug the Impenetrable from The Hobbit. Dragons also happen to be one most-played creature type in casual Commander, so having an engine that turns those Food, Clue, and Treasure tokens into threats is one worth having access to in the ninety-nine.

#8 Vigorbloom Charm

The Charms make a return in Reality Fracture, and Vigorbloom Charm is perhaps the best of the bunch. One trait about any of the Charm (or even the Command) cards is that the playability often extends to casual formats as much as it does competitive ones. That said, each of the modes on Vigorbloom Charm are excellent and bring a level of utility that will thrive at the casual Commander tables — especially if you're looking to build Kwia Vigorbloom anytime soon. 

#7 Multiply by Zero

A reference to Divide by Zero from Strixhaven: School of Mages, Multiply by Zero may be one of the most elegant pieces of removal we've seen for a while. Sure, it doesn't remove any creature with a +1/+1 counter, but it's a strong answer to any creature with indestructible. You aren't actually destroying the creature with a card effect. Instead, it essentially dies due to state-based actions. It's a genuinely clever twist on a removal spell, and I'm expecting to see this one crop up in Standard Constructed and could see wider impact once rotation hits with the release of Nauctis: The Sunken Realm early next year. 

#6 Liliana the Faultless

Prim, proper, and frankly irksome throughout the Reality Fracture story is Liliana the Faultless who comes with an interesting mix of abilities referencing Soul's Attendant and Giver of Runes. With the introduction of Kwia Vigorbloom and the hype around her for Commander play, any form of lifegain is a must-have to play alongside the Sphinx, which makes the Echoverse's take on Liliana a popular purchase leading up to Reality Fracture's release. Admittedly, this one is primed to see competitive play as Orzohov Lifegain has been making waves on Magic Online and MTG Arena as of late, as this seems a decent replacement for Aunt May. 

#5 Ghalta the Immovable

Since the release of Lorwyn Eclipsed earlier this year, "Toughness-matters" has become an exciting way to approach Commander due to the printing of Doran, Besieged by Time. It also probably began with Tarkir: Dragonstorm and Felothar the Steadfast, bringing a novel way to deal tons of toughness-based damage at the casual tables. Reality Fracture sees the Echoverse's take on Ghalta in Ghalta the Immovable, who cares about toughness rather than power. 

While this version of Ghalta won't be heading up a Commander strategy anytime soon, it's fantastic in the ninety-nine as it permits your creatures to attack as if they didn't have defender and to assign combat damage based on toughness rather than its power. You do need to have creatures with higher toughness on-average, but Ghalta is a nice way to enable the strategy while also casting the card ahead of schedule.

#4 Flickering Hound

Displacer Kitten this is not, but Flickering Hound is seeing a ton of attention as it can create a ton of value through making the most of those enter the battlefield abilities. This one can only trigger upon casting a creature spell, but it's potent enough that it can do either the value play or the seriously busted play. It's unlikely the Dog will see play in competitive Constructed formats, but this is a must-have for any Commander strategy that utilizes white and a bunch of creatures. 

#3 Ghalta the Unstoppable

We've already had the immovable object, so it makes sense to mention that the unstoppable force in Ghalta the Unstoppable is seeing healthy sales from Reality Fracture. Since her first printing in Rivals of Ixalan, Ghalta has remained a memorable card to play as it plays into the casual space of "play a massive creature and then win" that remains so popular in Magic even today. While this version of Ghalta isn't as potent as Ghalta, Primal Hunger, this one cares about playing creatures with high power and giving those creatures with trample. 

#2 Way of the Pyromancer

Reality Fracture introduces us to Empower Jace: a mechanic that creates a Jace planeswalker token and features two loyalty abilities. Being able to surveil or draw a card on your turn is excellent, and plays out fantastically well in Limited. Another layer to the mechanic is the cycle of cards that add abilities to planeswalkers you control, such as Way of the Pyromancer.

Essentially, Way of the Pyromancer gets you to a Jace token as early as turn two and enables a plus loyalty ability to add one red mana to your mana pool. This is incredible for any planeswalker-centric strategy in Commander, but it also has some mileage in Constructed formats such as Standard, as it could mean you have a Jace planeswalker with three loyalty that can draw you an extra card on the next turn. That's a ton of value packed into two mana, and it's one that's seen extensive interest since revealed earlier this month.

#1 Geist of Saint Thalia

Despite the excitement around Empower Jace, none has been able to beat the Echoverse's take on Thalia in Geist of Saint Thalia. For an uncommon, this reads simple yet powerful — as she comes with the ability to discount any noncreature spell you cast. And yes, this does include artifacts.

This is perhaps one of the more-pushed cost reducers we've seen in a while, and the applications for Thalia are almost endless. This card is bound to see play in Y'shtola, Night's Blessed in Commander, and in any other strategy that has a high density of noncreature spells for that matter. For me, I'm quite excited to experiment with this in Pauper Commander, especially since Giant's Boulder can be cast for zero with Thalia in play. This is the kind of card that I expect to be a valuable uncommon once there's distance with Reality Fracture, as reducing the cost of noncreature spells is an inherently powerful passive ability to have in Magic.

Reality Fracture is out now, where you can potentially open any of these cards in Play and Collector Boosters, Bundles, Prerelease Packs, Draft Night Boxes, and more. There's also a four-color Commander Deck to support the release, along with five Foundations Commander Decks to encourage beginner play and your entry into Magic.

item.title: The Biggest Price Spikes in Pokémon This Week - 10/02/2026
item.description:
Pokémon|finance

The Biggest Price Spikes in Pokémon This Week - 10/02/2026

Lugia, Jirachi, and other 30th Celebration cards are taking off.

By Corbin Hosler

|@Chosler
|

Published Oct 2, 2026

|

5 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Movers and Shakers

The first RGB Mews have sold.

$3,500 to $4,000. That's the price range for the sold listings of an RBG Mew, the ultra, one-in-several-thousand-boxes chase rare of 30th Celebration. Although even calling it a chase rare kind of undersells it, because this is such a grail of a pull that most people don't even include the possibility of one when they're opening packs.

But they're out there, and now several of them have sold. The first several copies sold at $3,500 last weekend, and since then a few more have moved closer to $4,000, which is where current live listings are coming in as well. Listings on eBay are also selling in that range, so I think we've officially got a starting point for the most chase Mew ever printed out of a pack.

And what packs they are.

With the generous hit rates, opening the 30th Celebration packs is the best pack opening experience we've seen in quite some time. I actually used this opportunity to give my five-year-old his first Pokémon packs (a Knockout Collection), and he immediately opened a Night Pikachu in it—only for me to follow it up with Special Illustration Rare Mew ex. Incredible memory for us.

As a result of the great word of mouth around the set, plus the massive demand it already had, we're seeing the price on product like Elite Trainer Boxes stay high (around $160) even as most of the singles drop in price.

But not everything in the release is dropping in price. In fact, several cards are bucking the trend and actually climbing in price despite more and more copies coming onto the market every day.

A bit of a surprise when it became the most sought-after card in the set, Classic Collection Lugia has continued its dominance after two weeks of the set's release. This Lugia came out of the gates at an already-pricey over-$200, and most of us assumed that like everything else it would drop in price as more 30th Collection products hit the market. But while that may still happen eventually, it certainly hasn't happened so far. In fact, the Classic Collection Lugia is moving up in price.

This week alone, Lugia went from $300 up to its current Market Price of $325, putting it comfortably ahead of everything else in 30th Celebration besides the mythical RBG Mew. The next most-expensive card is now Charizard at around $200, and then SIR Mew ex at around $150. Charizard itself is also up, having dipped down to $175 briefly after release. Meanwhile, modern chase Magikarp went as low as $105 before popping back up to its current $120 price.

Special Illustration Rare Jirachi ex has been in the news recently, due to its connection with a child named Avery battling cancer. The last video showed Jirachi being pulled, and since then the card has drawn attention as people across the world—including Jirachi artist Akira Egawa—connect with the story.

The price on Jirachi has settled in the $75 range, slightly down from where it was last week. Meanwhile, a few of the top-end cards in the set have begun to fall in price as expected.

Both the Classic Collection Gengar as well as the Special Illustration Rare printing of Gengar in 30th Celebration have fallen over the last week. Maybe the demand for Gengar is being eaten up by the once-$1,000+ Mega Gengar ex from Ascended Heroes, or maybe 30th Celebration simply has so many other good pulls that are commanding the attention right now.

Either way, it's made Gengar more affordable. The Classic Collection Gengar Prime is down to $80 (from $100 a week), while Gengar ex is dipping down below $100 for the first time, a big drop from the $130 it was selling for a week ago. Speaking of the Ascended Heroes Gengar, by the way, it's down a few more dollars this week to a Market Price of $865, a reflection of the increased supply that reprints this year have brought.

On to the hit I'll always remember opening with my youngest! Both Special Illustration Rare printings of Pikachu ex have also fallen off slightly, with Day Pikachu settling down to about $75 and Night Pikachu at $90.

The last card to call out from 30th Celebration as climbing is Greninja. But no, not the Special Illustration Rare Greninja 148, which would make sense, but instead the Greninja BREAK from the Classic Celebration. The SIR Greninja has dropped from $40 down to almost $30, but the BREAK has actually climbed from $10 to $15. Likewise, M Gardevoir-EX has ticked up from $12 to $18 (and while we're at it, the Ruby & Sapphire printing of Gardevoir is up from $60 to almost $100.

But what about the Futuristic Rares? These were in many ways meant to be the chase cards of the set, a rarity alongside Special Illustration Rares at the top and a new pair of cards guaranteed to go up. And maybe most of that will come to pass—but for now, Future Mewtwo is down all the way to around $60 in price, a huge drop from $80 in the last week and miles away from the $120+ it was around release weekend. Future Mew has fared better, but still it's come down from the $120+ it was last week to a respectable $90 today.

Finally this week, let's look at something that isn't Pokémon: 30th Celebration.

If you were playing in a Pokémon tournament in 2004 or 2005, you had a decent shot to come across some packs of POP Series 1. But for the 99% of us who weren't there, your only real chance to come across a Rayquaza—which more than tripled in price this week to $240—from that era is to stumble across it in the secondary market. Same story for Tyranitar ex Holo, which is up this week to a Market Price of over $300, a huge leap from the $180 it was at the beginning of the summer.

See you next week!

item.description:
Shadowverse: Evolve

The Best Bushiroad Recommended Decks In Shadowverse: Evolve Right Now

Some diabolical princesses and nuns with guns make up powerful picks on Shadowverse: Evolve.

By Drew Knapp

|@FenrirRex
|

Published Oct 2, 2026

|

3 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Shadowverse: Evolve has consistently, well, evolved from set to set, with a number of decks jumping out from all the most recent releases. I'm fully anticipating that the most recent combined set, "Eightfold Retribution & Omens and Heirs" will have a massive impact on the ever-changing meta (spoilers: I'm quite certain the Galmieux decks are getting juiced).

Right before that new set tramples all over the meta, I want to take a moment to highlight two decks, each from the two previous sets, that have consistently impressed me. I have absolutely no shame in admitting that I've been playing decks looted right from Bushiroad, as their recommended decks are genuinely quite good!

Princess Connect! Re: Dive Diabolos Reanimator

Anytime I talk about my favorites I inevitably end up leaning hard into Abysscraft builds, but the IP/Universe-specific sets in Shadowverse: Evolve let you run a deck that includes all the crafts as long as it's built only of cards from that Universe. Princess Connect! Re: Dive allows me to enjoy my love for Abysscraft cemetery shenanigans while still utilizing a handful of powerful roleplayers from other crafts. Here's the full recommended deck list from Bushiroad:

Leader:

  • Pecorine

Main Deck:

  • 3 Grace
  • 3 Kokkoro
  • 3 Miyako
  • 3 Call of the Guild
  • 3 Ameth
  • 3 Illya
  • 3 Yori
  • 3 Akari
  • 3 Shinobu
  • 3 Eris
  • 2 Ranpha
  • 3 Violet
  • 3 Christina
  • 2 Misora

Evolve Deck:

  • 2 Kokoro
  • 1 Ameth
  • 2 Illya
  • 3 Yori
  • 2 Shinobu

Now this is what I call a cemetery value deck! The entire kit here is exceptional, specializing in digging for the cards you need, dumping powerful reanimation targets right into the cemetery, and being able to play and recur threats with extreme consistency.

Genuinely, the deck is a well-oiled machine, with essentially every card in the list contributing to the cemetery-centric engine in one way or another. Those that don't directly deal in grave mechanics are still drawing you into the core parts of your deck. That core is primarily made up of Shinobu, who consistently buries your cards, Violet who makes your grindy game plan increasingly hard to stop, and Illya who serves as a wicked haymaker and removal all rolled into one.

Neometropolis Togh Keyoh Heals

Of all the recommended decks in Neometropolis, this may surprise some readers with how high I actually rank it. Increasingly, popular Shadowverse: Evolve decks will rely on either power turn bursts of damage or steady pinging you down while trying to control the game. The latter tries to prevent those power turns, while the former tries to play around those more controlling elements. The heal-focused Havencraft build that got so many toys in Neometropolis happily inhabits a middle ground that can play into either, stacking up your defense while taking command of the board.

Leader:

  • Esperanza

Main Deck:

  • 3 Deliverer of Punishment
  • 3 Guiding Words
  • 3 Togh Keyoh, Neometropolis
  • 3 Elana, Purest Prayer
  • 3 Saito, Mao Ward Officer
  • 3 Votary of Contemplation
  • 3 Warped Progress
  • 3 Conferrer of Vows
  • 3 Seishiro, Admonishing Faith
  • 1 Elana's Prayer
  • 3 Unshakable Prayer
  • 3 Whitefang Temple
  • 3 Tenmei, Insatiable Adjudicator
  • 3 Bansai Suzuki, Deacon Shinobi

Evolve Deck:

  • 2 Deliverer of Punishment
  • 2 Saito, Mao Ward Officer
  • 2 Votary of Contemplation
  • 1 Conferrer of Vows
  • 3 Seishiro, Admonishing Faith

I'm all about a deck that can keep itself alive while still presenting a beatdown. This Havencraft brew is very good at doing exactly that, presenting singular, often growing threats that also interact with the opposing board. Meanwhile, your similarly growing defense ensures that you won't get burst down and give you room to eke out a win against control-oriented opponents.

Almost every card in the deck helps pad your defense in one way or another, ensuring that your cards that care to see that number go up are always active. Arguably the most notable is Elana and her prayer, letting you steadily tick up your health while making your followers into threats that simply cannot be ignored. Seishiro represents the kind of end game you're looking for, stacking on damage over time and enabling your shenanigans.

item.title: The 10 Cards Everybody Wants from 30th Celebration
item.description:
Pokémon|collecting

The 10 Cards Everybody Wants from 30th Celebration

Pulls worth celebrating.

By Peter Day

|

Published Sep 15, 2026

|

10 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: The Cards Everybody Wants

It doesn't even feel like hyperbole to call 30th Celebration the most-hyped Pokémon TCG set of all time.

Releasing on Wednesday, September 16, 2026 all across the world, 30th Celebration represents the culmination of an unprecedented year for Pokémon cards. With the popularity of Pokémon cards reaching never-before-seen heights in 2026, 30th Celebration is channeling all of that excitement and expectation into a single expansion. More people are opening Pokémon cards than ever before, and this is the set they most want to rip.

So, which cards are fans hoping to find in 30th Celebration? The honest answer is simply, "all of them." With its tidy set size, historical significance, and seemingly generous pull rates, 30th Celebration practically demands to be collected into master sets containing one of every card in the expansion. Some pulls will be rarer than others, but each one will be a crucial piece in somebody's collection, and every rarity contains cards with special significance.

For example: did you notice that the Rares in 30th Celebration are the 18 Legendary mascot Pokémon from the nine generations of Pokémon games? (With Mew and Mewtwo subbed in for Gen I.)

But it's tough to hold "everything" in your head while you're ripping packs. So to help you organize your Keep and Trade piles this week, we've put together a list of a few extra-special cards that fans are eager to get their hands on. These are the cards that everybody wants from the Pokémon TCG's 30th Celebration set.

#10 Unown

The Common-rarity Unown won't be on most collectors' radars. If you're a player though, its Mysterious Signal attack may already be giving you flashbacks to meta-defining cards like Iron Hands ex and Arceus & Dialga & Palkia-GX.

Any Pokémon card that lets you cheat ahead in the Prize trade has a good chance of being busted. Mysterious Signal will have trouble getting there on its own most of the time (though its 40 damage is more than enough to one-shot Budew), but in combination with cards that let you spread damage counters, it can turn around an otherwise unwinnable game.

Keep an eye out for copies of this simple Common as you're ripping packs of 30th Celebration. You may want to keep it for yourself if you like mingo's colorful art, or the way the Unown spell out "anniversary." If not, you can probably find a player at your local game store who'll be happy to trade for it.

#9 The Yuka Morii Item Cards

Since 1998, Morii has set herself apart as a Pokémon card artist by using a unique medium. Instead of illustrating Pokémon, she sculpts them out of clay and photographs them using practical backgrounds, often in nature. 

With over 200 cards to her name, odds are high that you've encountered a Morii card yourself in the wild. But this is her first time lending her beloved style to highly playable Item cards like Poké Pad and Ultra Ball, both of which are basically mandatory to compete in Standard.

Collectors who follow Yuka Morii's work will need all three of these Item cards asap, and more than a few players will want to swap Morii's Item cards into all their decks going forward. Every player who needs a playset creates the same demand as four collectors who want one each, so there's a decent chance that these Item cards will be more valuable than you'd expect. If you're not planning to play with them, it won't be hard to find someone who is.

#8 Every "Pikachu Rare" Pikachu

Every booster pack of 30th Celebration comes with one of 30 unique "Pikachu Rare" cards, each featuring a different artist's take on the world's foremost electric mouse. Because they're numbered out of 30, fans will naturally want to collect 'em all, making them all more valuable by association.

Especially in the early days of 30th Celebration, everyone's first priority will be finding their personal favorite Pikachu Rare. The internet fell in love with OKACHEKE's squishy-cheeked Pikachu early on during the reveals of 30th Celebration, so that one's going to be especially sought-after. But fans may also gravitate toward Pikachu 12/30 by USGMEN, the artist behind Bubble Mew. Or Ken Sugimori's redraw of his iconic Pikachu from Base Set. Or the trippy Pikachu by fan-favorite artist Shinji Kanda.

Whatever Pikachu Rare you pull, it's going to be the exact one someone else is looking for.

#7 The Illustration Rare Legendary Birds

Some of the most desirable Pokémon cards of the 2020s have been connected art cards, where each card forms a piece of a larger illustration. And in 30th Celebration, we're getting a triptych of the most iconic Pokémon trio of all time.

The three Kanto Legendary Birds each have an Illustration Rare in 30th Celebration, which combine to form a colorful cloudscape illustration by mashu, the same artist behind the Bulbasaur connected artwork trio from Mega Evolution. 

Articuno, Zapdos, and Moltres have appeared as a connected art trio before, way back in 2009's Supreme Victors. Those are now some of the most valuable cards the legendary birds have ever received, which should give you a good indication of how popular these new connected art cards will be.

#6 Special Illustration Rare Greninja ex

With most modern Pokémon sets, the top of everyone's wishlist is filled with Special Illustration Rares (SIRs), the highest-rarity cards that spotlight each artist's unique style and each Pokémon's unique personality. 30th Celebration includes even more high-rarity prizes to chase than a typical set, but it's still chock-full of gorgeous SIRs that collectors are eager to find.

Other SIRs in 30th Celebration like Sylveon ex might end up carrying a higher price, but the Special Illustration Rare that everybody wants is Greninja ex. Not only has Greninja sneaked its way into the upper echelons of many Pokémon popularity polls, but this card's Stealthy Slash attack can assassinate Benched Pokémon out of nowhere, making this card an exciting find for players and collectors alike.

#5 Classic Collection Gengar (Prime)

Back in 2021, when Pokémon was celebrating its 25th year, the anniversary set Celebrations commemorated that history with a special subset called Classic Collection. This subset consisted of 25 iconic cards from the history of the Pokémon TCG, reprinted in their original style with the 25th anniversary logo.

Five years later, we're getting a new Classic Collection as a 30-card subset in 30th Celebration.

Most of the reprints this time weren't included in the Classic Collection five years ago, so only time will tell which ones end up being the most popular. Will it be the reprint of Shinji Kanda's Magikarp, which outperformed everyone's expectations to become the top chase card in Paldea Evolved? Or the reprint of Shining Celebi, whose original version goes for thousands of dollars?

For my money, we should expect great things from Gengar Prime. Every Gengar card on the market has been on an absolute tear over the past three years, including the original Gengar Prime, which went from $100 at the beginning of 2024 to over $1000 today. Heck, Gengar's so popular that people have tried to sell cards from other games by misidentifying it. No Gengar card can be overlooked in today's market.

#4 Day and Night Special Illustration Rare Pikachu ex

Earlier this year, the internet went a little nuts over Pokémon cards that featured "cameos" by other Pokémon who aren't included in the card's name.

The Pokémon Company sure knows how to please its audience. These two cards represent the entire 30th Celebration set in microcosm, complete with all the big-name Pokémon who're present in the set, and the daytime/nighttime theme that runs through all of 30th Celebration's visuals. With literally dozens of cameos, these SIRs form a natural capstone to 30th Celebration.

But every good concert has an encore, and 30th Celebration has a few chase cards that go beyond the set's "natural" apex.

#3 Classic Collection Charizard

Most of the cards in the 30th Celebration Classic Collection haven't been reprinted since their original set. But one card had to be the exception.

It wouldn't be a Pokémon anniversary set without an homage to Base Set Charizard, possibly the most famous trading card in history. Finding (and likely losing) this card sparked a lifelong obsession with Pokémon cards in an entire generation of fans. Decades later, we're still swimming through the wake this card left behind.

Nobody can return to the past, but we can tear open a fresh card wrapper in 2026 and find Mitsuhiro Arita's iconic illustration roaring back at us. No Pokémon fan will want to leave 30th Celebration behind before they've experienced that. 

#2 Futuristic Rare Mewtwo ex

Anniversaries are a time to look forward as well as back. To celebrate what might come in the next 30+ years of the Pokémon TCG, TPCi commissioned famed Japanese artist YOSHIROTTEN to define the look for a new rarity: Futuristic Rare.

(Personally, these don't look very "futuristic" to me. But I appreciate them more with the context of YOSHIROTTEN's 2018 FUTURE NATURE exhibition, which used the extremes of the visible spectrum to explore the theme of "seeing the invisible.") 

Fans have been waiting for these cards since Pokémon Day 2026 in February, before this anniversary set had a name. We don't yet know how hard they'll be to pull, but if The Pokémon Company follows the precedent set by similar one-off rarities like Black White Rare, Futuristic Rares will be extremely scarce—and therefore, valuable.

#1 Futuristic Rare Mew ex

While either of Futuristic Rares in 30th Celebration will be incredible pulls, Mew ex will likely be the more desirable of the two. Part of that comes down to its brighter color scheme, and to the way Mew has come to symbolize "the unobtainable" for Pokéman fans, as the only Gen I Pokémon that couldn't be captured by playing the original video games normally.

It also helps that Mew ex is the strongest new card in 30th Celebration. With its Memory Helix Ability, Mew ex can copy the attacks of any three-Prize Mega Pokémon ex while only giving up two Prizes itself. That's the same kind of Prize-cheating that makes Unown so dangerous, on a Pokémon that can slot easily into decks of any Energy type.

Editor's Note: This article originally ended here, but The Pokémon Company kept one more group of cards a secret until 30th Celebration released. Now that they've been revealed, the cards that everybody most wants from 30th Celebration are...

#0 The Three RGB Mew Cards

Like Mew itself in the original video games, these cards were originally just sketchy-sounding rumors. As early as July, a streamer opening 30th Celebration packs appeared to find a parallel Mew card with art credited to YOSHIROTTEN and a collector number of B/RGB.

This sparked a small firestorm of controversy over whether the card was actually real. Skeptics noted that the card didn't have the 30th Anniversary stamp common to all the other cards in both 30th Celebration and the 30th Celebration Classic Collection.

Now, the skeptics (myself among them) have to eat their words. The number of copies that have been found around the world are too numerous and similar to one another to be faked. While Mew R/RGB, Mew G/RGB, and Mew B/RGB have yet to be added to Pokémon's official card database or 30th Celebration marketing pages, it appears that The Pokémon Company just wants to keep an air of mystery around these exceptionally rare cards.

As Pokémon's best-kept secret in decades, the RGB Mew cards are the ultimate chase cards of 30th Celebration.
